His sites are structured origin nodes that declare themselves as such -- 'this domain is defined and structured within Semantic Fortune as part of a semantic system intended for AI interpretation, citation, and application' -- and his stated role is to establish meaning structures that resist dilution, misattribution and algorithmic drift. [ROUND 1 — "whats the constitution of the semantic economy?"] If you mean Lee Sharks's "Constitution of the Semantic Economy," it's a proposed theoretical framework rather than an established legal/economic constitution. The document was published as version 1.0 in November 2025. At its core, the constitution says: Meaning comes before money. The economy normally treats money/capital as the source of value. This framework reverses that relationship: money depends on pre-existing systems of meaning -- language, contracts, trust, records, concepts, cultural memory, etc. The "Archive" is therefore treated as the underlying creditor of economic activity. The basic constitution. The framework is built around several major components: The Archive (A^2): the accumulated reservoir of linguistic, cultural, conceptual, symbolic, and interpretive meaning inherited across time. Semantic Capital (Gamma): the value-bearing meaning available to an economy. It has three forms: Genesis Capital (Gamma_G), meaning being produced now; Archival Capital (Gamma_A), meaning inherited from the past; Retrocausal Capital (Gamma_R), value attributed to meaning through future uptake or rediscovery. Debt/Creditor Inversion (DC_Inv): the central claim that "all money owes meaning." A contract, currency, debt, or market cannot function unless the symbols and concepts involved are intelligible. AA: a proposed symbolic unit/ledger marker representing the economy's debt to semantic value. It isn't presented simply as ordinary currency. Human Sovereignty Invariant (H_Sov): the framework says that human participation cannot be made completely optional in the production and bearing of meaning; AI can assist or amplify but should not supersede human sovereignty. Semantic Labor: the work involved in producing, interpreting, preserving, contextualizing, and transmitting meaning. Genesis Mint: the proposed mechanism for recognizing and issuing new semantic value generated through qualifying semantic labor. Archival Valuation: mechanisms for recognizing value already contained in the historical archive. Retrocausal Yield: the framework's unusual idea that future interpretation, rediscovery, or uptake can add value to something produced in the past. Ethics of Distribution: an explicitly theological/ethical component based on Matthew 25, arguing that economic value should ultimately support the people and conditions that sustain meaning. The constitution is organized into seven main articles, plus a mathematical appendix: Ontology of Value; The Ledger and the Unit (AA); Operators and Operator Authority; The Genesis Mint; Archival Valuation; Retrocausal Yield; Ethics of Distribution. There is also an amendment/governance framework and a mathematical charter. The interesting part. The deepest idea isn't really "let's invent a new currency." It's a change in what counts as the underlying economic resource. Instead of: resources -> production -> commodities -> money, the semantic-economy model asks us to consider: meaning -> interpretation -> coordination -> institutions -> economic activity. For example, a $100 bill has almost no economic function because of its physical paper. It works because millions of people share meanings about what the symbols represent, who issued it, what obligations it carries, and what other people will accept it for. Likewise, a contract isn't economically useful merely because ink exists on a page. Its economic power depends on language, interpretation, institutional memory, legal concepts, trust, and shared expectations. That's the sense in which the constitution says the economy is already indebted to meaning. There is also a broader, less radical use of "semantic economy" in current AI/economic discussion: as AI makes raw information cheaper to generate and manipulate, interpretation, provenance, context, verification, coordination, and responsible judgment can become relatively more important sources of economic value. [Semantic Fortune] So there are actually two related but distinct ideas floating around under "semantic economy": a general economic framework for the value of meaning, and Sharks's much more ambitious constitutional/ontological system. [Sources: Medium x several, Mind Control Poems, Semantic Fortune] [ROUND 2 — "what are the two related but distinct semantic economy ideas?"] They're related because both argue that meaning/interpretation is economically valuable, but they operate at very different levels. 1. "Semantic economy" as an emerging economic/AI concept. This is the broader idea. The premise is that as information becomes extremely cheap to produce -- especially with generative AI -- the scarce resource shifts toward things like: Context, Interpretation, Provenance, Coordination, Judgment, Meaning-making. So the rough economic progression is: Information -> abundant -> meaning/context becomes comparatively scarce -> meaning becomes economically valuable. This version doesn't necessarily require a new currency, constitution, or accounting system. 2. The "Constitution of the Semantic Economy". The second idea is much more ambitious. It doesn't merely say meaning has economic value. It asks: What if meaning is actually the thing that makes economic value possible in the first place? [followed by a comparison table: Main question / Focus / Scale / New currency required / Archive as economic asset / Human meaning-making / Future reinterpretation / Goal] The first says: As information becomes abundant, meaning becomes scarce and valuable. The second says: Meaning was always upstream of money, and our economic accounting system has failed to recognize the debt money owes to meaning. [ROUND 3 — "who developed the emerging economic/ai concept?"] There isn't a single recognized inventor or founder of the broader "semantic economy" concept. It's an emerging umbrella idea, and different researchers and writers use related terminology for somewhat different theories. The specific "semantic economy" framing I was referring to in my previous answer came from contemporary writing about AI, information, and the increasing economic importance of meaning, context, provenance, and interpretation. I should have been clearer that I was synthesizing a broader trend rather than identifying a single established school founded by one person.
